articles.title: Mapúa University launches 9 new MBA elective tracks for professionals
articles.summary: Consider this your sign to get that Master's degree

blocks.text: Consider this your sign to get that Master's degree

Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by Mapúa University and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

With the rise in AI adoption, digital transformation, and demand for evolving strategic management skills, Mapúa University, in collaboration with Arizona State University (ASU), is expanding the Master of Business Administration (MBA) program with new industry-focused elective tracks under its E.T. Yuchengco School of Business.

The move is also in response to growing demand from MBA applicants and students for more defined areas of expertise. The E.T. Yuchengco School of Business recently introduced nine elective tracks under the MBA program covering Financial Technology, Supply Chain Management, Digital Marketing with AI, Hospital Administration, Healthcare Administration, Public Health and Technology, Educational Management, HR Management, and Tourism and Hospitality Management.

While an MBA offers a general foundation in core business principles, the E.T. Yuchengco School of Business is sharpening its value propositions to meet the market’s demand for focused learning and expertise.

According to Donn Enrique Moreno, dean of Mapúa University E.T. Yuchengco School of Business, working professionals pursuing an MBA degree aim to deepen their expertise and broaden their career growth and opportunities. Moreno cited examples of those who would benefit from this development.

“The Educational Management elective track is designed for professionals seeking leadership and management roles in educational institutions, while Healthcare Administration provides a pathway for professionals preparing to lead increasingly complex and technology-driven healthcare organizations,” Moreno explained.

The nine industry-focused elective tracks currently offered remain highly relevant to the demands of today’s rapidly evolving business landscape. The Financial Technology elective track continues to play a vital role in financial planning, investment management, and digital finance strategies for organizations operating in a global economy.

Likewise, the Digital Marketing with AI elective track reflects the growing integration of technology and data-driven information in brand management, customer engagement, and market analytics, enabling businesses to drive sustainable growth amid ongoing market transformations.

blocks.caption: ELEVATE YOUR OPERATIONS LEADERSHIP. Gain the competitive edge to streamline complex global systems with Mapúa’s targeted elective tracks.

blocks.text: The Supply Chain Management elective track addresses the increasing demand for professionals capable of developing efficient logistics and operations strategies that optimize the flow of goods or services from suppliers to end consumers. Similarly, the HR Management elective track continues to be important as organizations place greater focus on talent development, workforce strategy, and employee engagement.

blocks.caption: LEAD SMARTER SUPPLY CHAINS. Master supply chain strategy and global logistics with Mapúa University’s MBA program, in collaboration with Arizona State University.

blocks.text: The modern healthcare sector also benefits from industry-focused MBA elective offerings. The Healthcare Administration elective track equips professionals with the competencies needed to navigate digital health innovations, emerging technologies, and expanding healthcare systems.

Complementing this, the Hospital Administration elective track prepares future leaders with a strong foundation in healthcare management, finance, legal and ethical guidelines, human resources, and information systems necessary for addressing contemporary challenges in the healthcare industry. Meanwhile, the Public Health and Technology elective track promotes adaptability by embedding technology such as AI, digital tools, and other related innovations into the core of public health education and practice.

Effective leadership, strategic planning, and management also remain essential in the education and tourism sectors. The Educational Management and the Tourism and Hospitality Management elective tracks are designed to prepare professionals for leadership and administrative roles, enabling them to uphold industry standards, respond to emerging challenges, and contribute to the continued development of their respective fields.

“The industry-focused elective tracks give our MBA students the opportunity to complement their core business and management education with courses aligned with their professional interests and career aspirations. Students may choose a track that is relevant to their industry or the leadership direction they intend to pursue,” he added.
Through these offerings, MBA students can tailor part of their graduate education to their professional goals, strengthening their readiness for leadership and career mobility across industries.

“Combined with ASU-enhanced global learning, digital readiness, and applied learning, these elective tracks strengthen our goal of developing business leaders who can respond to the evolving needs of industries locally and globally,” Moreno concluded.

Mapúa University is the flagship university of iPeople, Inc. — the education joint venture between majority owner House of Investments, the listed holding company of the Yuchengco Group of Companies) and Ayala Corporation. The two conglomerates share an empowering common goal to make world-class education accessible to as many Filipino students as possible

Discover how Mapúa University E.T. Yuchengco School of Business, in collaboration with ASU, can help advance your career with an MBA. For more information and to apply, visit campaign.mapua.edu.ph/ub-asu/apply-for-mapua-mba-2627/. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 'Hero' pilot stabbed by other pilot on Israel-bound plane, Israeli PM says
articles.summary: Passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and safely landed the plane in Saudi Arabia.

blocks.text: A pilot has been arrested after he stabbed the other pilot on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv and "apparently tried to crash the plane", Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said.
Passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control of the Flydubai aircraft, landing it safely at an airport in Tabuk, northwestern Saudi Arabia, with more than 170 people on board.
The passengers, who were almost all Israeli, arrived later on Wednesday in Tel Aviv on a repatriation flight.

The stabbed pilot, named as Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, has been taken to hospital but is reported to be in a stable condition. Netanyahu praised him as a "true hero" of "extraordinary bravery".

"Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster," Netanyahu wrote on X.
"He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals."
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar was in a stable condition in hospital.
Image source, EPA
Passengers arrived in Tel Aviv after their original flight was forced to land in Saudi Arabia

No motive for the incident has been given and the pilot was under investigation in Saudi Arabia, Netanyahu told Fox News on Wednesday night, before he was expected to be taken back to the United Arab Emirates (UAE), where the flight took off from.
Israel was "likely" to contribute to the investigation, the prime minister added.
US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu following the incident, saying it seemed as though the attacker was "perhaps a terrorist" or there were other reasons behind the attack.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has also called it an "attempted jihadist terror attack", without giving any details.
Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben-Gurion Airport in Israel.

Around two and a half hours into its journey, data from flight tracking website Flightrader24 reported a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia, dropping more than 17,000 feet (over 5,000m) in less than two minutes.
Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code reporting a hijacking.
Around 20 minutes after these codes were signalled, the plane looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.
Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.
Shortly after the incident, the Israeli and Saudi Arabian air forces dispatched fighter jets, while Netanyahu held urgent consultations.

blocks.caption: Map showing the route of Flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The plane departed Dubai at 03:05 GMT and flew northwest across Saudi Arabia towards Israel. Near the Israel-Jordan border, the aircraft declared a general emergency at 05:31 and a hijacking alert at 05:38 before turning away…

blocks.text: Initial media reports suggested a fight had broken out between the aircraft's two pilots, causing the rapid descent and landing.

However, in the hours after the plane touched down in Tabuk, eyewitness accounts and a statement by Netanyahu confirmed one of the pilots had stabbed the other and, according to the Israeli prime minister, "apparently tried to crash" the aircraft.

He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member entered the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".
Two on-duty crew travelling on the flight were then able to land the plane safely, Flydubai said.

In an address on Wednesday evening, Netanyahu called the situation "a very serious security incident" and said Israeli security forces were "maintaining close contact with the relevant authorities to ensure the continued safety of the passengers".
Unlike Israel's defence minister, Netanyahu did not give a motive for the incident.
"I salute these heroes who demonstrated extraordinary resourcefulness and courage," he added. "They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster."

blocks.caption: A woman smiles and embraces a person draped in an Israeli flag as passengers who were on the FlyDubai aircraft bound for Israel from the United Arab Emirates are greeted by their friends and family, as they arrive at the Ben Gurion International Airport.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters

Flydubai said in a statement that "an altercation occurred in the flight deck" and the flight was "successfully secured by on-duty Flydubai crew travelling on the flight, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely at Tabuk airport".

An airline spokesperson added: "Our immediate priority is to ensure the ongoing safety, health, and wellbeing of all passengers and crew members involved in this incident and support the official investigation."

The passengers who had been on board flight FZ1073 arrived in Tel Aviv at around 18:40 local time (15:40 GMT). They were greeted at the airport by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags.
A number of people were "very emotional and crying as they came off the plane," a paramedic from Israel's ambulance service told the BBC.
One passenger, Yaniv Hayun, met Netanyahu and told him how he and others on the flight had restrained the attacker.

"The pilot who was stabbed was simply very close to the door, so it was hard for us to open it," Hayun said in a video posted on social media by the prime minister's office, but before the stabbed pilot - now identified as Machchhar - collapsed, he was able to open the door.
Yaniv said he put the attacker, who was trying to disable the plane, in a chokehold before other passengers helped pin him down.
He added that he "pulled the controls" of the plane and after it levelled out, another pilot took over control.
Zvika Meness, another passenger, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan News that he and other passengers tied the attacker up "with his own zip ties and with the multimedia headphones".
He said: "There are children and families here who have been through a very severe, highly traumatic event."

image.caption: 'The pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it,' Hegseth said [FILE: July 27, 2026]Image: Evelyn Hockstein/REUTERS

blocks.text: US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday that the United States military has slashed the number of its generals and admirals by 20%.
He made the announcement while addressing junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia during what he called his "State of the Force" address.
"The number-crunchers say we fired 10% of the generals and admirals across the force," Hegseth said, adding: "We've also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10%."
"So yes, 20% reduction across the board," he noted. "The media calls that a purge. I call it accountability, and long overdue."
How the US is merging artificial intelligence and warfare
Cutting the fat or a purge?
The address came a year after a similar speech to top officers in which Hegseth said the US military was too fat, too focused on leftist "woke" ideas, and in need of major shake-up.
Since the start of Donald Trump's second term as president early last year, a number of top military personnel have been forced out of their positions.
Trump, for instance, fired the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Charles "CQ" Brown, without explanation in February 2025.

Other senior officers pushed out include the heads of the US Army, Navy and Coast Guard, the general who headed the National Security Agency, the vice chief of staff of the US Air Force, and a Navy admiral assigned to NATO.
Hegseth has insisted the president is simply choosing the military leaders he wants.
But Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns about the potential politicization of the US military.
Some members of Congress have called the latest cuts to the general ranks a "purge" that will take years to rebuild.

"He's got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military,” Democratic Senator Mark Kelly told the Associated Press. Kelly is a former Navy combat pilot who has been critical of Hegseth. "He's purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it's going to take a generation to recover from it."
Republican Senator Mike Rounds, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he wanted to understand Hegseth's reasoning.
"If it's simply a matter of eliminating a very heavy top, there may be some validity to it, but I want to see it first," Rounds said.
Fighting Iran war, can US military sustain a long conflict?
What Hegseth said about the new command
On Wednesday, Hegseth also announced his intention to create a new drone-focused warfare command, which would oversee the rollout of autonomous and robotic capabilities.
He said that "the pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it."
The defense secretary pointed to Ukraine's use of drones to combat Russian forces to underscore how warfare and battlefield tactics are changing.
"Ukraine's lesson is not that one type of drone wins wars, but rather the need for a purpose-built system that maximizes the ability to adapt," Hegseth said.

To study the future of warfare, the secretary unveiled a task force led by tech billionaire Elon Musk, former Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Palmer Luckey, co-founder of Anduril Industries.

He said the work "will be focused on discovering, developing and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes." The Pentagon chief pointed to the need to dominate "any future battlefield, from under the Earth to beyond the moon."

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency issued an advisory to airlines to avoid Saudi airspace, according to a bulletin posted on its website on Wednesday, Septembet 30, following a recent increase in attacks by the Iran-aligned Houthis.

The latest advisory on Saudi Arabia does not mention Wednesday’s incident involving a diverted flydubai airliner, and the EASA said it will continue to monitor the situation to assess whether there is an increase or decrease in risk for EU airlines in the country.
The EASA, in a separate bulletin, recommended that flights not operate within the airspace of Jordan at any altitude or flight level, a change from a previous advisory to exercise caution.

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

articles.title: Oasis take legal action to stop sale of unheard recordings valued at more than £1m
articles.summary:
Tapes made in the 90s, including candid conversations between Noel and Liam Gallagher, which were expected to sell for up to £1.6m

A collection of unheard Oasis recordings, including 63 live…

blocks.text: A collection of unheard Oasis recordings, including 63 live shows, hours of rehearsals and candid conversations between Noel and Liam Gallagher, has been pulled from auction after legal action taken by the band.
In September Littleton Auctions in Worcestershire, England, listed the collection made by the band’s former sound engineer, Huw Richards, with a guide price of between £1.2m and £1.6m.

Richards worked with Oasis from the release of their 1994 debut Definitely, Maybe until 2001. The collection of 209 DAT tapes, 73 analogue cassettes and three MiniDiscs were being sold by the sound engineer’s son, Owain Richards.

“Littleton Auctions confirms that the Oasis recordings known as The Desk Tapes have been withdrawn from our October 3 auction in light of legal proceedings,” the auction house’s managing director, Ben Homer, told the BBC.
“We are very disappointed that we cannot offer this significant archive as planned.”

In an interview with the Times in September, Owain Richards, also a sound engineer, called the collection “a piece of history”. He said the audio remained in sufficiently good condition, but as Oasis retained the intellectual property rights, the recordings can’t be released by a potential new owner without the band’s cooperation.
“It is true that Oasis have sued me and my father to try to prevent the auction of the tapes made by my father many years ago,” Richards told the BBC on Wednesday.
“We have agreed to postpone the auction [of the tapes] to enable the legal dispute to be resolved either by litigation or otherwise in an orderly way.”

Littleton Auctions will continue with the auction on Saturday, with other music memorabilia up for sale including an original Kangol Oasis tour parka from Richards’ collection, plus signed Nirvana photographs, autographs of two of the Rolling Stones members, and a guitar signed by Brian May.
“The rest of the sale is unaffected and will take place as normal,” said Homer. “We respect the legal process and will make no further comment on the proceedings at this stage.”

Last month, Noel and Liam Gallagher attended the world premiere of documentary film Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger at Venice film festival followed by its UK premiere in London. The band also recently announced its Live ’27 world tour following their successful reunion tour in 2025.
Oasis have been approached for comment.

articles.title: Police search for additional victims as two bodies discovered in California
articles.summary:
Officials investigating missing persons case find bodies in remote area of Lancaster, north of Los Angeles

Law enforcement officials are looking for additional victims after two bodies were…

blocks.text: Law enforcement officials are looking for additional victims after two bodies were found on Tuesday in a remote area of Lancaster, California, a small city about 70 miles north of Los Angeles, the Los Angeles Times reports.

Authorities found the bodies in a shallow grave while they were investigating a missing persons case, according to KTLA. Outside of the sheriff’s department investigating the discovery of the remains as a homicide, little is known about the two people who were found in the shallow grave.
On Wednesday, KTLA’s helicopter captured authorities and staff with the medical examiner’s office digging in new areas near where the bodies were found.

Lancaster is a city of just over 170,000 people, according to the most recent census data. The city is unincorporated and therefore under the jurisdiction of the county sheriff. Like much of the nation, Lancaster has seen a substantial decrease in homicides, with killings declining by 35% between 2024 and 2025, according to the city.
The Los Angeles sheriff’s department did not immediately respond to the Guardian’s request for comment on the case.

articles.title: COA asks Ombudsman to look into Albay flood control project
articles.summary: State auditors earlier flagged the use of funds for the repair and reconstruction of a consolidation dam in Ligao City, Albay, where a concrete revetment was built instead

blocks.text: COA. The Commission on Audit in Commonwealth Ave., Quezon City.
Rappler
State auditors earlier flagged the use of funds for the repair and reconstruction of a consolidation dam in Ligao City, Albay, where a concrete revetment was built instead

items: The Commission on Audit has requested the Office of Ombudsman to investigate a P9.97-million flood control project in Ligao City due to issues with a payment of P5.77 million to BDL Construction and Supply.

A notice of disallowance was issued against the regional Department of Public Works and Highways for failing to rebuild a consolidation dam after Typhoon Bebeng, leading to the disallowance of funds allocated for the project.
The COA ruled that using the project funds for a different construction (a concrete revetment) violated government procurement laws and could lead to potential legal consequences for those involved.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Audit asked the Office of Ombudsman to look into a P9.97-million flood control project in Ligao City, Albay.

In a 15-page decision dated July 28, state auditors upheld a 2022 ruling by the COA Region V on the notice of disallowance it had issued against the regional Department of Public Works and Highways’ (DPWH) payment, worth P5.77 million, to construction firm BDL Construction and Supply.
The notice of disallowance held liable BDL Construction and Supply, as well as then-DPWH regional director Danilo Dequito and chief engineer Efren Manalo.

In 2012, the DPWH regional office had awarded a contract worth P9.97 million to the company for the repair and reconstruction of a consolidation dam and a scoured riverbank at Pinit Foot Bridge in Ligao City, both of which were damaged by 2011’s Typhoon Bebeng (Aere).

In 2013, the COA Regional Technical Services Office conducted a site inspection and found that the consolidation dam had not been rebuilt, even after the contractor said it had finished the project. The COA regional office then disallowed P5.49 million — the budget assigned to the consolidation dam — plus miscellaneous expenses, totaling P5.77 million.

Manalo had appealed the notice of disallowance since a concrete revetment was built near where the original consolidation dam was supposed to be repaired and reconstructed. The agency had argued it would be unjust enrichment on the part of the government if the contractor was not paid for this replacement project.

The COA en banc, however, said using the consolidation dam project fund for the concrete revetment violated the provisions of Republic Act No. 9184 or the Government Procurement Reform Act, and the project’s funding source, the 2010 General Appropriations Act, and was “tantamount to disbursing government funds without a valid appropriation.”
State auditors said it could have also violated Article 220 of the Revised Penal Code, and that there could be basis to investigate for possible indictment for technical malversation. – Rappler.com

articles.title: [Time Trowel] Can DNA tell us who Filipinos are?
articles.summary: Filipino identity cannot be reduced to DNA or ancestry percentages; it is shaped by complex histories of migration, contact, and culture.

blocks.text: A trowel (/ˈtraʊ.əl/), in the hands of an archaeologist, is like a trusty sidekick — a tiny, yet mighty, instrument that uncovers ancient secrets, one well-placed scoop at a time. It’s the Sherlock Holmes of the excavation site, revealing clues about the past with every delicate swipe.

The search for the “real Filipino” has moved from textbooks and nationalist mythmaking into the language of DNA. Type “Filipino DNA” into YouTube and the “ancestors” appear almost immediately. One video posted this year claims that “Filipinos Aren’t Asian — DNA Proves We’re the Original Pacific Islanders.” Another promises to explain how “Filipino DNA was formed over thousands of years.” Bloodlines, ancient ancestry, migration, and genetic percentages are increasingly presented as answers to where Filipinos came from and, by extension, who Filipinos are.

Full disclosure: I collaborate with geneticists, and some of my archaeological research intersects with population and plant genetics. Genetics has expanded what we can learn about migration, ancestry, interaction, and population history. Problems arise when genetic ancestry becomes a stand-in for ethnic identity or when population history is used to answer the question of who Filipinos are.

Consumer DNA tests can make ancestry categories seem more definite than they are. In March 2026, 23andMe announced 144 genetic groups associated with the Philippines and neighboring regions. These tools help people trace family histories and connections across populations. Problems begin when their categories make identity appear to be encoded in DNA.

DNA researchers estimate ancestry by comparing genetic data across sampled populations using statistical methods. The results depend in part on who is included in those samples, how large and representative the reference groups are, and which statistical methods are used. If the samples or methods change, the estimate can change too. The DNA itself has not changed.

Across archaeology, history, genetics, and related fields, the concept of Austronesian has been attached to pottery, migration, genes, ancestry, food, entire populations and, heck, even dogs. The word can end up mixing language, biology, and culture into a single category. It starts to sound as though Austronesian names a biological population and that hundreds of millions of people across a large part of the world descend from the same ancestral group.

Scientific writing sometimes adds to this problem. A 2025 review, for instance, discusses the genetic origins and migrations of “early Austronesian peoples.” The term may be useful shorthand for a particular study, but it can easily suggest that speakers of Austronesian languages also constitute a biological population.

A genomic study of 1,028 individuals from 115 Indigenous Philippine populations identified evidence for at least five major migrations into the archipelago over roughly the past 50,000 years. This was not one population arriving with a ready-made package of genes, farming, language, and culture. People arrived at different times, encountered populations already living in the islands, intermarried with them, and contributed to the population histories we see in the Philippines today.

There was no single migration that produced Filipinos, nor was there an original Filipino population waiting in Taiwan, southern China, Sundaland, or somewhere else on a migration map. People migrated, married, traded, fought, and joined other groups. Genetic studies can trace some of these movements, but the patterns they identify are statistical reconstructions of population history. They cannot be read as direct evidence of language or culture.

In addition, a 2021 study found that Ayta Magbukon individuals carry the highest measured levels of Denisovan ancestry reported among the populations studied. The Denisovan finding contributes to our understanding of population history and encounters between modern humans and archaic hominins. It offers little basis for defining who counts as Indigenous or Filipino.

It is, thus, very easy to be trapped in the search for an “authentic” prehispanic Filipino in genetics, as if biological ancestry could identify who counts as more original or more Indigenous. In the Philippines, indigeneity emerged from historical circumstances shaped by colonial expansion, state formation, displacement, relationships to land, and the ways communities maintained political and cultural identities under changing regimes. Treating it as a biological inheritance risks tying culture and belonging to blood. The US National Academies has warned against treating race, ethnicity, ancestry, and genetic similarity as interchangeable categories. Human genetic variation does not divide people into the fixed groups that such labels often suggest.

Archaeology has often helped reproduce the idea of bounded, culturally uniform peoples. Yet the archaeological record gives us little reason to expect a culturally pure population before 1521 CE. Pots and foods moved across communities. Technologies were borrowed and often remade. People migrated, married, traded, fought, and joined other groups. Languages spread across populations with different ancestries, while communities maintained some practices for generations and changed others along the way.

The idea of an “authentic” prehispanic Filipino says as much about what people want to find in the past as it does about the past itself. A population untouched by migration, contact, intermarriage, or cultural change would be difficult to locate archaeologically. The people who lived in the islands before Spanish colonization were already part of long histories of movement and contact.

Filipino identity came out of those histories and the centuries that followed. It took shape through communities, colonial experiences, resistance, accommodation, language, migration, kinship, food, religion, labor, and political change. None of this can be reduced to an ancestry percentage or traced back to a biologically pure Filipino.

Genetic reconstructions of population history do not tell us who people were. Genetic studies attempt to reconstruct population history. They do not recover identity. Searching our DNA for the original Filipino assumes that such a biological Filipino once existed. The same problem appears when we go looking for an Austronesian in our genes. We are not our DNA tests. – Rappler.com

Stephen B. Acabado is professor of anthropology at the University of California-Los Angeles. He directs the Ifugao and Bicol Archaeological Projects, research programs that engage community stakeholders. He grew up in Tinambac, Camarines Sur.

articles.title: Daredevil Jaan Roose prepares to walk slackline high above central Seoul
articles.summary:
Estonian will navigate narrow ribbon, 160 metres long and 120 metres high, near the city’s famous Gwanghwamun palace on Thursday

Estonian aerial athlete Jaan Roose will attempt to cross a…

blocks.text: Estonian aerial athlete Jaan Roose will attempt to cross a 160-metre long highline suspended 120 metres above central Seoul on Thursday.

Roose, a three-time slackline world champion, will step out on to a narrow polyester ribbon between the Koreana hotel and the Dong-A Media Center, near the capital city’s famous Gwanghwamun palace and square.
The 34-year-old has made a name for himself slacklining dramatic urban environments, such as his 185-metre high feat between Qatar’s Iconic Towers.

In 2024, he became the first person to slackline the strait of Messina between mainland Italy and Sicily, completing the 3.6km traverse despite a fall near the end, caught by his safety harness. Earlier this month, he covered 14.7km over 12 hours on a line above the Danube in Bratislava, Slovakia.

Large crowds in Seoul are expected to watch Roose walk the slackline – twice, at 1pm and 4pm local time – if the weather allows. The walk will be postponed if average wind speeds reach 10m/s or gusts hit 15m/s. Today’s forecast is sunny with light breezes.

blocks.caption: A woman in Warsaw, Poland, watches Estonian slackliner Jaan Roose cross a highline suspended above the city in 2026. Photograph: Marek Antoni Iwańczuk/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Roose said a visit in 2022 to South Korea inspired his Gwanghwamun walk.
On that trip, Roose encountered jultagi, Korea’s traditional tightrope walking, which Unesco added to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2011.
Unlike tightrope walking elsewhere, jultagi is as much comedy as acrobatics. The walker sings, jokes and dances on the rope, trading banter with a clown on the ground as musicians play.

articles.title: California bans child marriage, a practice still legal in 32 US states
articles.summary: Gov Gavin Newsom called it a "long overdue measure to protect young Californians".

blocks.text: Stodden said she would "keep fighting until children are protected from marriage in all 50 states".

She was married to actor Doug Hutchison - known for roles in The Green Mile, A Time to Kill and I Am Sam - in 2011, spurring headlines internationally over the controversy and appearances on several reality programmes in the US, including the VH1 series Couples Therapy.
Other survivors of child marriage also applauded the new law.

"California has sent a clear message to the world today," Brittany Bee, a former child bride, told the BBC. "A message of hope for all children that they may be free from systemic violence. That they may choose their own path."
Bee told the BBC she was wed at the age of 17 to escape an abusive home - only to then be allegedly abused by her adult husband.
"I was just going from one prison to another," she explained. "People have the audacity to tell me that I made a choice - kids, they can't consent."
Bee and other child marriage survivors have been working for years to have child marriages banned in California and across the United States.
About a decade ago, the practice was still allowed across all US state but more and more states have been altering laws. California is the 18th to ban it since 2018.
In the state, there had been no legal age to wed, allowing children to get married as long as their parents consent and a judge signs off on the nuptials.
There was also no mechanism for people under 18 to get divorced and many girls say they were trapped in abusive and predatory relationships.

Unchained At Last, an advocacy group fighting to end child marriage across the US, said about 9,000 girls were wed each year in California and that almost all child marriages involved girls to adult men.
Advocates say that many in the US don't even know that child marriage is legal in so many US states, nor that is has led to allegations of abuse.

Sara Tasneen, who says she was forced to marry a man nearly twice her age when she was 15 years old, told the BBC that it felt "surreal" to finally have the state recognise that child marriage should be banned. She says she started lobbying for this herself in 2017.
She was introduced to her husband the morning of their arranged marriage.
"I was forced to be his wife and that day, my entire life changed," she told the BBC. She became a mother the following year, at the age of 16, and dropped out of school.
"To have seen the arc of this bill come to fruition has been a marathon," Tasneen said. "I'm just grateful that kids cannot get married after January 1, 2027 in California."

articles.title: Vic Rodriguez mulls MR after SC junks Sara Duterte impeachment threshold petition
articles.summary: Vic Rodriguez mulls MR after SC junks Sara Duterte impeachment threshold petition

blocks.text: Published October 1, 2026 8:56am

Former executive secretary Vic Rodriguez said Thursday he is considering filing a motion for reconsideration of his petition against the Senate impeachment court’s decision on the voting threshold in the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Rodriguez made the statement in an interview on GMA News’ Unang Balita after the Supreme Court on Wednesday dismissed his petition questioning the impeachment court’s action.

“We are considering the filing of a motion for reconsideration, and we are given 15 days from receipt of the resolution. As of today, while this interview is ongoing, we have yet to get a copy of the resolution,” he said.
Rodriguez’s petition questioned the authority of the Senate as an impeachment court to set the specific number of the voting threshold for conviction in impeachment.
The SC En Banc dismissed the petitions filed by Rodriguez, Berteni Causing, and lawyer Ernesto Francisco Jr. on procedural grounds, including lack of standing and prematurity.

Last week, the Senate impeachment court voted to base the two-thirds vote to convict Duterte on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings."
This set aside the July 6 ruling by presiding officer Senator-judge Francis "Chiz" Escudero, who set the votes needed to convict at 16, which is two-thirds of all 24 senators.

Thirteen senator-judges voted in favor of the motion put forward by Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo, who sought reconsideration of the July 6 ruling after some senators became unavailable to participate in the impeachment trial.—AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Passengers foil bid to crash plane, Israel says, after co-pilot stabs pilot
articles.summary: The incident involves 174 people on board, with one injured pilot hospitalized, and draws attention from international leaders, including US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin…

items: A flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, after a co-pilot attempted to crash the aircraft by stabbing the pilot, but passengers and crew successfully intervened to prevent a disaster.

Israeli officials are investigating the motive behind the attack, which has raised concerns about aviation security in the region, prompting Israel to implement stricter checks on pilots flying into the country.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Passengers on a Flydubai flight reached Israel safely on Wednesday, September 30, after customers and crew foiled a co-pilot’s attempt to crash the aircraft, Israeli officials said, in a struggle that began when he stabbed the pilot and sent the jet plunging nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds.

Passengers and crew entered the cockpit, overpowered the co-pilot and enabled a second pair of flydubai pilots who were aboard the flight to land the jet safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, Israeli officials said.

More than 10 hours later, the passengers arrived at Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport aboard a flydubai replacement aircraft, with several describing the episode as a miracle and recounting a frantic struggle to prevent a catastrophe.

blocks.caption: ORDEAL. Passengers who were on the FlyDubai aircraft bound for Israel from the United Arab Emirates, which was diverted to Saudi Arabia following an emergency signal, arrive at the Ben Gurion International Airport, in Lod, near Tel Aviv, Israel, September 30, 2026. Reuters

blocks.text: Israeli officials said the attacker’s motive aboard flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv remained under investigation. Israel and the United Arab Emirates, which includes Dubai, signed the Abraham Accords normalizing relations in 2020.
The incident sharpened concerns about global aviation security in a region scarred by years of conflict, prompting Israel to tighten checks on pilots flying into the country.

“I just can say that it was a miracle. It was awful, crazy, and we thank God that we survived it, we didn’t think we will make it but thank God we are in Israel. We are back home. And we are happy to see everyone here,” passenger Lital Shachaf said.
Israel’s ambulance service said a 51-year-old man was taken to an Israeli hospital to be treated for injuries to his upper body. The man was in a “mild condition,” it said.
Describing the event as “a serious security incident,” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Saudi authorities would interrogate the co-pilot.
Flydubai said in a statement that the underlying reasons for the event remained unknown and warned against “premature speculation.”
An Israeli official identified the co-pilot as an Omani national. There was no immediate comment from Oman.
Israeli officials applauded the passengers, who they credited with avoiding a much more serious disaster.
Netanyahu said there were 174 people on board the flight from Dubai, most of them Israeli nationals.

US President Donald Trump said he spoke “at length” with Netanyahu on Wednesday about the incident. He proceeded to give reporters in the Oval Office a detailed account of what happened, adding: “This is the story that I heard — I don’t know if it’s true, but that’s the story that I got from Bibi (Netanyahu).”

A Netanyahu spokesperson told Reuters that the wounded captain, identified by the Israeli leader’s office as Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, was covered with blood on the floor when he managed to click the release to open the cockpit door.
Passengers who entered found the co-pilot bashing at the plane’s control panel, the spokesperson said.

“This is something you do without thinking, just running to save your daughter’s life, your family’s life,” said Asaf Rajuan, one of the passengers who helped restrain the attacker. He spoke with a forehead still bloodied from the struggle.
Netanyahu’s office released a video showing the prime minister at Ben Gurion Airport giving a hug to another passenger, Yaniv Hayun, who his office said “broke into” the cockpit.
“I see you and I see a lion – a big hero,” Netanyahu told the man, who was still wearing the blood-stained shirt he had on during the flight.
Flydubai operates daily return flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv, a route that is popular among Israeli nationals. The flight path normally uses airspace over Saudi Arabia and Jordan.

It is not the first time a flight between Israel and the UAE has landed in Saudi Arabia. A flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv made an emergency landing in Riyadh in September 2025 due to a medical incident, Israeli media reported at the time.
Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport, where the plane landed, said both pilots had been hospitalized after sustaining injuries.

The incident heightened security fears in Israel weeks before Israelis vote in the first election since the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attacks, with Israel’s security figuring prominently in the campaigning.
Responding to the incident on X, far-right security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir wrote, “Terrorism is a devil with whom no agreement must be reached.”

Israeli media published conflicting reports on the incident, with some outlets reporting that a pilot had tried to crash the passenger plane in an alleged suicide attempt. Some Israeli media outlets initially identified the pilots as Omani and Emirati nationals, while others said they were Russian and Ukrainian.

“Every pilot that is going to be flying into Israel, we are going to know the pilots’ identities, know who they are, and do some type of security check,” Doron Spielman, a Netanyahu spokesperson, told Reuters.

Netanyahu met on Sunday with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan during a rare visit to the Gulf country. Israel and the UAE have forged close security, military and economic ties since establishing diplomatic ties.

Israel provided the UAE earlier this year with Iron Dome air-defense systems and Israeli personnel to operate them, helping defend against Iranian attacks launched after Israel and the US began strikes on Iran.

The UAE government had yet to comment on the flydubai incident, while the Dubai state-owned airline said an “altercation” occurred in the cockpit and the flight subsequently diverted to Tabuk, where it landed safely. The UAE’s aviation regulator, the GCAA, said the flight “experienced a security incident that was brought under control.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Gavin Newsom signs laws to protect California workers from AI threat
articles.summary:
Democratic governor sharply critical of Donald Trump for not passing comprehensive federal AI regulations

Governor Gavin Newsom signed laws Wednesday aimed at protecting California workers…

blocks.text: Governor Gavin Newsom signed laws Wednesday aimed at protecting California workers from the threats of artificial intelligence , including potential job losses and workplace surveillance.

The laws ban employers from using the technology to predict a worker’s emotional state by using their biometric data, require employers to send written notices to workers if AI is responsible for mass layoffs and ban employers from relying on AI to decide to fire someone.

The Democratic governor also signed an executive order to require state agencies to continue to refer to the technology as “artificial intelligence” instead of the term “super intelligence” as Donald Trump recently ordered US diplomats to use.
“AI should expand opportunity – not come at the expense of workers and families,” Newsom said in a statement. “As this technology reshapes the workplace, California is putting people at the center.”

He sharply criticized Trump at an hour-long event with reporters Wednesday for not passing comprehensive federal AI regulations at a time when industry leaders are warning about the technology’s risks. Trump said Tuesday that top tech leaders signed a voluntary accord to “self-police” AI development.

The governor signed a law this month requiring operators of AI chatbots to perform risk assessments before rolling them out and an executive order requiring the state to consult with experts to further improve oversight over the industry.
“We have to do a lot more in the absence of federal leadership,” Newsom said, leaving the door open for the possibility of calling lawmakers back for a special session to further tackle the issue.

The news conference came on Newsom’s last day to sign or veto bills before he terms out in January. He started the event by signing a law creating a tax credit program aimed at helping local news organizations – including newspapers, digital outlets and TV stations – hire and retain journalists. Newsom criticized what he called Trump’s assault on a free press, pointing to the president’s barring of news organizations from the White House.

Newsom also spoke about the upcoming midterms, which will decide control of Congress. He involved himself early in that fight by leading Democrats last year in a redistricting battle to improve their chances of winning more House seats. He’s said repeatedly that the stakes are high if his party doesn’t succeed in November.
“There will not be a free and fair election in 2028 unless we take back the House of Representatives,” he said Wednesday.
Asked if he had set a deadline for himself to decide to run for president in 2028, Newsom hedged, saying: “That moment will arrive when it arrives.”

Former Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris, who, like Newsom, hails from the San Francisco Bay Area, has also said she’s considering running for the job in 2028. Newsom told CNN recently that he would not run for president if she entered the race. He said the two have not spoken since that interview aired.

Newsom weighed in on a proposal to temporarily raise taxes on billionaires that will be on the ballot in November, which he’s consistently opposed. He said he respects supporters of the measure, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who are committed to addressing income inequality in the country.
“He’s spot on about the balance between the rich and the poor,” Newsom said. “On this issue, we fundamentally disagree.”
Newsom’s remarks came hours before a gubernatorial debate between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton.
“You’re going to ask me, ‘Are you going to watch the debate?’” he said. “No.”

articles.title: Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss, threatening water supplies
articles.summary: Scientists say such rapid melting is no longer surprising given the pace of climate change.

blocks.text: Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.
More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".
They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.
The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.
There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed.
But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.

The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting.
Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear.
"It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.
One of the most ominous findings is what researchers observed at measurement sites at the highest elevations, where temperatures are lowest and glaciers are typically snow-covered.
Even as high as 3,500 metres above sea level, scientists found no snow remaining at the end of summer.

"At some glaciers we've seen four metres of ice loss at the highest point, where they should be covered by several metres of winter snow at this time of the year," said Huss, from Glacier Monitoring Switzerland.
Snow is like glacier food - and under stable conditions some of it would eventually compact into ice.
But if no snow survives the summer, it cannot replace the ice lost to melting at lower, warmer elevations. The glacier will starve, shrink and eventually disappear.
"Glaciers are complex because they gain mass at the top and they flow downstream, so there is a lot of physics," explained Maussion.
"But in its simplest form, what we see right now is that we took an ice cube out of the fridge and it's just melting in front of our eyes."
Scientists say the climate is now too warm for many Alpine glaciers to survive.
Some, like Plattalva in eastern Switzerland, have already disappeared.

articles.title: Palace: Baste Duterte seems ‘unconcerned’ about VP Sara’s GenCorp stake
articles.summary: The Palace spokesperson stressed that public officials should not use the Arias doctrine to protect their own interests or hide potential negligence of their families and allies.

blocks.text: Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte testifies as a hostile witness on the 31st day of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial at the Senate in Pasay City on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026.
The STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang said Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte seems "unconcerned" about Vice President Sara Duterte’s financial interest in GenCorp Industries Inc. following his appearance as a witness in his sister’s impeachment trial.

At a press briefing on Wednesday, September 30, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro declined to make a conclusion as to whether Baste was covering for Duterte after claiming in his testimony that he only learned about GenCorp through the trial.

“Hindi natin masasabi. Hindi natin mabibigyan ng anumang paghuhusga ang kanyang statement. Ang ipinakita lang niya kahapon ay wala siyang alam. Wala siyang alam. Hindi niya inalam at parang wala siyang pakialam,” Castro said.
(We can’t say. We can’t give any judgment on his statement. What he showed yesterday was that he knows nothing. He is clueless. He did not bother to find out and he seems unconcerned.)

Baste appeared in the Senate impeachment court on Tuesday, September 29, to testify on the alleged unexplained wealth of the vice president, particularly on what the prosecutors claim as a conflict of interest involving GenCorp’s contracts with the Davao City government.
He was later declared by the Senate impeachment court as a hostile witness.
The prosecutors’ arguments stemmed from the P34.2 million worth of 15 contracts in Davao City awarded to GenCorp from 2022 to 2026. Baste, on the other hand, claimed there were 19 contracts.
The vice president is listed as a stockholder in GenCorp, which was also declared in her 2024 and 2025 statements of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN).
Good faith

Castro also said Baste appeared to defend himself after Senator-judge Panfilo “Ping” Lacson brought up the Arias doctrine during the trial, asking the witness if he had been informed by his counsel regarding it.
“Parang lumalabas na pinagtanggol niya ‘yung sarili niya as a mayor. Inangat niya yung sarili niya as a mayor,” Castro said.
(It appears that he is defending himself as a mayor. He held himself in higher regard as a mayor.)

The Arias doctrine was established in a landmark Supreme Court ruling in 1989, which states that heads of offices can rely in good faith on the decisions and signatures of their subordinates when approving routine documents.
Castro noted that the Arias doctrine can only be invoked in an isolated case and cannot be used to cover up repeated anomalies or signs of irregularities that a public official should have noticed.
The Palace spokesperson also stressed that public officials should not use the doctrine to protect their own interests or hide potential negligence of their families and allies.

“Hindi lang ito para kay Mayor Baste Duterte. Sa lahat na po ng pinuno, dapat maging alerto rin kayo. Hindi pwedeng gamitin itong Arias v. Sandiganbayan para lang isagip ang sarili niyo,” Castro said.
(This is not just for Mayor Baste Duterte. To all head officers, you should be alert. The Arias v. Sandiganbayan cannot be invoked to save yourselves.)

articles.title: Kristi Noem, former Trump homeland security chief, files for divorce
articles.summary:
Noem cites irreconcilable differences in filing that comes after husband Bryon Noem involved in tabloid scandal

Kristi Noem, who was fired by Donald Trump after a rumbustious stint as…

blocks.text: Kristi Noem, who was fired by Donald Trump after a rumbustious stint as homeland security secretary, is divorcing her husband, Bryon Noem, after 34 years of marriage, citing “irreconcilable differences”.
The divorce claim “for settlement purposes only” was disclosed in court records filed in Hamlin county, South Dakota, the state of which Noem was previously governor.
The document was signed by Noem’s lawyer, Michael Sabers, on 6 April – just over a week after the Daily Mail published pictures of her husband wearing inflated fake breasts under a spandex shirt.
At the time, Noem issued a statement saying she was “devastated” by the images, adding that “the family have been blindsided by this”.
The papers were only filed in court this week, according to the New York Times.
Sabers confirmed Kristi Noem had filed for divorce and said she would reserve further comments for the legal process.
Tim Bottum, Bryon Noem’s attorney, said his client was “saddened that the marriage is ending” and would welcome the opportunity to share his perspective if court proceedings were necessary.
“Bryon’s priority is to protect the family and move forward as loving parents and grandparents,” Bottum said in a statement.
The revelations came weeks after Noem had lost her job at the department of homeland security.
The state of her marriage had already been subject of speculation amid rumors that she was in a relationship with her aide at the department, Corey Lewandowski.
In a Capitol Hill on 4 March, a Democratic member of Congress asked her openly whether she had sexual relations with Lewandowski.
Answering under oath, Noem – who was accompanied to the hearing by her husband – dismissed the question as “tabloid garbage” but did not say no.

She was fired the following day after Trump was reportedly angered by her answers to questions about a taxpayer-funded publicity campaign that promoted Noem’s image. Noem told the committee that Trump had signed off on the spending.

Noem was replaced by Markwayne Mullin as homeland security secretary after a controversial period that had included the shooting deaths of protesters Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis during an immigration enforcement surge. Noem came under intense criticism after calling Good and Pretti “domestic terrorists”.
Noem, 54, married Bryon Noem, 56, in 1992. They have three adult children.

articles.title: US Supreme Court allows execution of Christa Pike to go ahead
articles.summary: The death by lethal injection was scheduled to happen earlier on Wednesday before a lower court paused the execution.

blocks.text: The US Supreme Court has cleared the way for Tennessee inmate Christa Pike to be executed, overturning a last-minute reprieve.

The killing by lethal injection was scheduled for Wednesday morning before judges from the Sixth Circuit Appeals court halted the execution. Tennessee's attorney general then immediately requested the Supreme Court to overrule the lower court's stay.
Pike, 50, has been awaiting execution since she was convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.
If the execution proceeds, Christa Pike will be the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. It was not immediately clear when the execution would take place.
Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh granted the application to vacate the stay of the execution. No explanation for lifting the stay was provided in the order.
The top court's three liberal justices - Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson - dissented in Wednesday evening's order.
Sotomayor wrote that she dissents because the decision cleared the way for Tennessee to execute Pike before her pending legal challenges to her conviction "can be properly considered".
"Tennessee's desire to expedite Pike's execution by a few days or even weeks cannot outweigh her 'fundamental interest in [her] own life," she said.

The latest ruling from the Supreme Court came just before 18:00 local time, hours before the state's execution order is set to expire at midnight. If time runs out the Tennessee Supreme Court will need to set a new execution date, the Associated Press reports.
In a ruling earlier on Wednesday, judges from the Sixth Circuit Appeals court paused the execution saying they needed more time to consider the arguments in Pike's case.
Pike's lawyers said that for years, the state of Tennessee argued in court that she had lied about being sexually abused as a child.
But at a recent hearing about her execution method, the state said it did not dispute she suffered sexual abuse and rape.

Pike's legal team asked the appeals court to send her motion back to the district court, arguing that if the federal courts based their ruling on the state's earlier claim that she was lying, then the federal review was affected.
Earlier this week, the Supreme Court refused to hear a different appeal from Pike.
Tennessee governor also denied a clemency request this week from the death row inmate.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

articles.title: Man arrested over alleged plot to attack Texas state capitol
articles.summary:
Suspect Benny Caldera Jr held on bond as officials say they received ‘credible’ information about Austin threat

A 40-year-old man was arrested early Wednesday on suspicion of plotting to…

blocks.text: A 40-year-old man was arrested early Wednesday on suspicion of plotting to attack the Texas state capitol, authorities said.
The Texas department of public safety said in a statement that it received “credible information about an individual planning a violent attack” for Thursday in Austin.
The tip came in Tuesday evening, and Swat officers made the arrest at about 3am on Wednesday at a residence in Converse, Texas, near San Antonio.

Benny Caldera Jr was jailed on a $75,000 bond. He could face charges including felony terroristic threat against a public servant, officials said in a statement. Messages were left seeking comment from an attorney listed for Caldera.

Officials did not provide details about the alleged plot, citing the ongoing investigation. Public safety officials notified state lawmakers about the threat and arrest early on Wednesday. The Capitol remained open during regular operating hours.
Texas senate secretary Patsy Spaw said in a notice that there will be increased security at the Capitol during the investigation.
Governor Greg Abbott said the state DPS was assisted by the FBI in making the arrest.
“Texas will NOT tolerate threats of violence against our Capitol,” the governor said in a statement on social media.

articles.title: BFP ‘secured’ majority to elect BARMM chief minister – spox
articles.summary: Negotiations to form the majority were immediately underway after the hotly contested race that resulted in a hung parliament

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) has already “secured” enough seats to form a majority in the first elected Bangsamoro parliament and elect a chief minister, BFP spokesperson Naguib Sinarimbo told Rappler.

Negotiations took place immediately right after the hotly contested race that resulted in a hung parliament. BFP got 32 seats, closely followed by the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) with 30 seats, and BARMM Grand Coalition (BGC) with 15 seats.

“While ‘yung work among political parties of creating a majority has started, ngayon nangyayari na ‘yon,” Sinarimbo said in a Rappler Talk interview. “And in our case, we’re confident we have the number.”
(The work among political parties of creating a majority has started. And in our case, we’re confident we have the number.)
“We already secured the majority to be able to elect the chief minister come October 30,” he added.

The elected members of parliament will hold their first session on October 30. BFP’s chairman Abdulraof Macacua, who is currently the interim chief minister, is the party’s bet to lead the Bangsamoro government.

Asked of his chances of becoming the region’s first elected chief minister after his proclamation on September 15, Macacua said: “Titingnan natin (We will see). Because being the chief minister, the majority will decide on that.”

Leaders of the BARMM Grand Coalition have met recently with the two biggest parties. Sulu Vice Governor Abdusakur Tan posted a photo with UBJP leaders – Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim and Mohagher Iqbal – on Monday, September 28.
Tan’s province was excluded from BARMM as a result of a Supreme Court ruling, but the official’s group remained active in the predominantly Muslim region’s politics.
“This high-level convergence highlights the power of dialogue and solidarity—working hand-in-hand toward a peaceful, inclusive, and prosperous future for the entire Muslim region,” said Tan.
A day after, BGC leaders met with BFP which included Macacua and Sinarimbo.
“Hindi kailangang magkapareho tayo palagi sa ating mga pananaw para makapagtrabaho nang magkasama,” Basilan Governor Mujiv Hataman said. (We don’t always have to agree on views to work together.)
These early, talks are a harbinger of what is to come. Governance through the parliamentary system would necessitate many negotiations, said Sinarimbo.
“Kasi ‘yung parliamentary system, ang nature niya talaga ay kailangan makipagkasundo ka sa ibang mga partido at ibang political actors in the region,” said Sinarimbo.
(The parliamentary system’s nature requires collaboration with other parties and other political actors in the region.)
“It cannot be an exclusivist party,” he said.

After the election of the regional chief minister, urgent matters that require the parliament’s focus are passing the 2027 budget and organizing the BARMM cabinet. Cabinet members, who will head ministries, will be selected from the members of parliament.
Sinarimbo said the system creates a challenge in finding members who have the skill set to both legislate and hold Cabinet positions.

“It’s difficult with the parliamentary system because there is fusion of legislative and executive work,” Sinarimbo said in Filipino. “It’s difficult to find individuals who have the skills to both do legislation and execution.”
Under RA 12317, the new set of officials elected in September 2026 will serve until June 30, 2031.

articles.title: The children dying in India's remote tribal heartland
articles.summary: At least 32 children have died in India's Balaghat district since May amid outbreaks of measles and malaria.

blocks.text: Warning: This article contains details some readers may find distressing
At about 3am one morning in May, Bamita Markam began convulsing.
The three-year-old had spent days with a high fever and angry red sores on her body. Her mother, Koushila, had first taken her to a doctor, who prescribed an ointment.
Bamita seemed to recover, then became ill again. A faith healer, called to the house in Matla village, gave her syrups and tablets. Nothing worked. By dawn, Bamita was dead.
"She cried a lot," Koushila recalls. "She convulsed all night." The family tried to make her drink water. At one point she vomited blood. They buried her in a jungle after midday.

Bamita's death was one of at least 32 child deaths recorded since May in a cluster of remote villages in Balaghat district in India's Madhya Pradesh state, officials say. The victims ranged from babies just three or four months old to an 18-year-old, and most were Baiga, one of India's 75 "particularly vulnerable tribal groups", external.
Officials attribute the deaths to mainly measles and malaria, possibly aggravated by malnutrition and delays in treatment.

They believe eight to 10 deaths were associated with measles, roughly another 10 with malaria, with several children suffering more than one infection. The precise cause of every death is less certain.

"I have never seen an outbreak like this. My father was a two-term lawmaker, and I have served three terms, but neither of us has seen so many children die in such a short time," Sanjay Uikey, who has represented the area since 2013, told me.
But disease is only part of the story. In remote, forested parts of Balaghat, where Maoist insurgency once took root, reaching a health centre can be a challenge in itself.

In the monsoon, the terrain can make that journey harder. Paddy fields glow against red earth and low, forested hills. Narrow dirt tracks wind between fields and mud homes, often becoming slippery and impassable in heavy rain.
The countryside is lush, but the homes are sparse. Most Baiga houses have low mud walls, rough timber and bamboo, and tiled or thatched roofs patched with plastic against the rain.

Some homes are accessible only by these tracks. Doctors investigating the deaths have travelled through the mud in tractors. On a recent visit, we walked nearly 2km (1.2 miles) uphill to reach some of the more remote homes. The surrounding jungle was dotted with the graves of children who had died.

The nearest state hospital, a 100-bed facility in Birsa, is about 70km away. For families without vehicles, reaching it can mean muddy tracks, a makeshift bamboo stretcher or a motorcycle - and a day's lost wages.
When Bamita became seriously ill, the family did not get her to hospital. It was raining heavily. The tracks were muddy and slippery, and the family had no way of transporting her.
"If I was able to take her to hospital she might have lived," Koushila says.
Her other daughter, Ankita, keeps asking what happened to her sister. The six-year-old has been told what many children in these villages are told: "Mata aa gayi" - the goddess has arrived.

For some Baiga families, some illnesses - like chicken pox - are seen as the arrival of a disease goddess, who must be appeased rather than treated. Families perform a seven to nine-day ritual of bathing and offering cool water and neem leaves to the local disease goddess. Many believe that treating the patient before the ritual is completed could cause death.
For weeks, such beliefs shaped how families responded to sick children. Then the scale of the deaths began to emerge.

On 21 July, Parshuram Dhurwey, a local village council chief, heard that two children in the same household in Bondari village had died. The next morning, he heard of another death. He called local officials and went to the area.
They found a grim picture.
"Every other child was sick," Dhurwey says. "They had fever, they had rashes. Many were undernourished."

When government medical officer Nimish Gautam arrived, he found severely dehydrated children. The first case he saw was a teenage girl with several days of fever and rash, whose blood sugar appeared dangerously low. Her family refused to let the health team examine her properly.

"Police were brought in to persuade them to take her to a health centre. The family still refused," Gautam told me. "They said if we took her for treatment, she would die. So we kept her under observation, and she recovered."
In one village, Dhurwey says, officials forcibly entered homes and took five seriously ill children to hospital. All recovered.

By the time the outbreak became unmistakable to local authorities, children had already been dying for weeks. By September, Dhurwey says, 10 children aged about 18 months to 14 years had died across the four villages in his council - Adori, Kundekasa, Bondari and Usri.

The symptoms were frighteningly similar and frustratingly non-specific: fever, rashes, weakness, dehydration and, in some cases, seizures. Some children had scabies, fungal infections or bacterial skin infections alongside suspected measles and malaria. In a district where malaria is endemic, external, fever could mean several things at once.

Sagnibai of Bondari lost two children within 24 hours. Her daughter, Lamnin, 12, died on 26 June. Her one-year-old son, Sahil, died the following day. A local healer told the family it was Mata. They also had no money or vehicle to take the children to a doctor.
Her husband, Samaroo Dhurwey, remembers nights in which the children's bodies seemed to be "on fire". They could not digest food. They died at home.

Mahasingh Parte of Matla village lost two children - a six-year-old girl and a four-year-old boy - within two days of each other. The family followed a faith healer's instructions. "He said don't take them to hospital," Parte recalls.

Parte is a landless farm labourer who earns about 200 rupees ($2; £1.58) on a good day, he said. Work is scarce in the monsoon, and although a small primary health centre is just 5km away, he had never been there. Poverty and remoteness had stacked the odds against his children.
The question of what was making children sick became harder to answer as the deaths mounted.

An investigation by the ICMR-National Institute for Tribal Health Research (NIRTH) tested 10 samples collected from the affected villages on 7 August. Six tested positive for measles; four were negative.

Measles is highly contagious, causing high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by a rash. Most children recover, but malnutrition can make measles far more dangerous, external, increasing the risk of pneumonia, severe diarrhoea and dehydration, and inflammation of the brain. The infection also weakens the immune system, leaving children vulnerable to other infections. Malaria can compound that risk.
But doctors cautioned that malaria did not necessarily follow measles, and not every fever and rash was measles. Instead, several infections and vulnerabilities collided.
"Sometimes there is no single factor behind the deaths," Gautam said. "There are malnourished children and there's zero health education and hygiene at home."

The Baiga villages are not entirely disconnected from modern India. Seasonal migration takes families to other states for chilli picking and other work. Children watch reels on smartphones, while many families have minimum single-bulb solar-powered electricity, bank accounts and, in some homes, piped water.
Yet malnutrition remains widespread, with children often poorly fed. A five-year-old who died recently of measles weighed around 5kg.
Gautam believes malnutrition is driven by early marriage and motherhood, with some girls becoming mothers at 16 or 17, when their bodies are still developing.

Closely spaced pregnancies, premature births and low birth weight can follow, while young mothers struggle to breastfeed and care for their children. Diet is another problem: many families rely heavily on rice and lentil soup, with too little protein and dietary variety. Studies on Baiga households have found widespread nutritional deficiencies, compounded by poor uptake, external of public services.
The gap between services on paper and on the ground was stark: the state response came weeks after deaths began, while health teams struggled to reach and persuade families.

Once the outbreak was recognised, health workers began door-to-door screening in affected villages. Mobile medical units carrying oxygen, nebulisers, suction equipment, malaria tests and medicines visited more than 20 affected villages.

One mobile doctor, Neeraj Sharma, says teams routinely saw more than 50 patients a day, about half of them children. They conducted 10 or more malaria tests daily, sometimes finding two positive cases a day.

More than 6,200 patients - mostly children - were eventually treated at home, according to Gautam. More than 630 were referred to district hospitals. About 600 returned home, while around 30 remain admitted.
Vaccination became an emergency response. Although official records suggested 90-95% coverage in some areas, health workers found children without records and families reluctant to vaccinate.

Authorities therefore offered the measles-rubella (MR) vaccine to all children under 15, regardless of recorded status. Of about 40,000 children identified in Birsa, roughly 27,000 had been vaccinated, Gautam said. Of the area's 180 villages, some 67 are predominantly Baiga and among the most vulnerable.
But vaccination is only one part of the protection children need. There are wider questions about whether basic nutrition and other health services are reaching those most at risk.

A 2024 audit by India's Comptroller and Auditor General found "serious irregularities", external in Madhya Pradesh's distribution of take-home rations meant to supplement the diets of children aged six months to three years, pregnant women and lactating mothers, including problems with beneficiary identification, production, transport and distribution.

The outbreak has now subsided. Officials say the last child death was more than two weeks before their late-September assessment, while teams continue visiting villages. In Kundekasa, a medical camp that once saw about 120 children a day was seeing fewer than 10.
Back in Matla, Bamita's mother speaks about the child who would ask for money for snacks, play with her sister and run inside whenever cars approached because vehicles frightened her.
"I had hope she'd study and make something of herself. I never regretted I didn't have a boy," Koushila says.
Then she looks at Ankita, the surviving sister.
"I want more kids," she says. "I feel alone. Ankita is alone. She keeps crying for her sister."
